picks.excerpt: Baroness Thangam Debbonaire argues the book trade must move past polarised 'for/against AI' framing and build practical licensing systems that fairly pay authors while acknowledging AI's utility — 'you have to ask the bigger philosophical question' about humanity's role. Delivered at the PLS conference.
picks.rationale: Strongest fresh pick: a named policy figure reframing AI licensing toward a practical author-pay framework — distinct speaker/angle from the 7/6 PLS 'AI copyright litigation' and 7/11 PLS licensing cards; credible on-list source, directly shapes how publishers/authors monetise and control work.

picks.excerpt: Reporting outcomes from the World Conference on Research Integrity Focus Track, the authors argue scholarly publishing urgently needs a single shared standard for disclosing AI use, replacing today's fragmented journal-by-journal rules that leave authors and editors guessing.
picks.rationale: Judged distinct from prior scholarly-AI cards — disclosure standardisation is a different topic than the 7/8 'making AI use traceable' (traceability) and the earlier peer-review theme. Actionable author/editor workflow norm from a credible on-list source.

picks.excerpt: At a July 7 Tokyo publisher briefing, Rakuten Books outlined a strategy centred on 'personalized discovery using Rakuten data and AI' for its 28M monthly visitors — an AI-recommendation push positioning its bookstore against Amazon.
picks.rationale: Held to meet floor 3: weak roundup-sourced item, but its lead (Rakuten AI-driven book discovery) is a distinct fresh retail-strategy story with an AI-recommendation hook — a different PP URL than the 7/13 'no single model' card, so no outlet-content repeat. Deprioritized behind the two credible picks.
